checked_sources.evidence: Opened IAU Taurus chart; it explicitly labels TAURUS and M45 in the charted sky region.

Opened; NASA lines 295–320 identify M45 as an open cluster in Taurus, give 445 ly and over 1,000 stars, describe visibility, Merope/radiation-pressure particle sorting, and state that the bright rays are an optical effect within the telescope.
Opened; IAU lines 799–810 defines constellations as bounded sky areas and distinguishes being within a constellation from membership in a drawn star pattern.

articles.finding: The draft correctly separates Taurus as an IAU-defined sky area from M45 as an open cluster. NASA directly supports 445 ly, more than 1,000 loosely gravity-bound stars, unaided-eye visibility under dark skies, Merope's radiation-pressure grain-size effect, and the telescope-internal origin of apparent rays. The self-check has a clear answer.

checked_sources.evidence: Opened IAU Pegasus chart; it labels PEGASUS, M15 and adjacent ANDROMEDA, so it supports the directional association without a false boundary inference.

Opened; NASA lines 295–328 identify M15 as a globular cluster in Pegasus at 33,600 ly and about 12 billion years old, describe its dense core and blue/orange stars, and identify Pease 1 as a planetary nebula—the gaseous shell of a dying star—visible within the cluster; lines 317–318 support binocular and Pease 1 wording.
Opened; IAU lines 803–810 supports the article's sky-region versus drawn-figure distinction.

articles.finding: The article treats Pegasus as a sky area and M15 as a distinct globular cluster. NASA directly supports Pegasus placement, globular-cluster type, 33,600-ly distance, about 12-Gyr age, dense core with blue/orange stellar populations, Pease 1 as a dying star's gaseous shell, and binocular visibility. The heading and self-check teach the intended object distinction without claiming every Great Square corner belongs to Pegasus.
